description: We began as an organisation for a non-profitable charity. However, even after this event ended we never stopped having the feeling of being a part of this organisation in our hearts, we competed as a team in many other competitions including the GCHQ coming 103rd in England. Now with the 2026 Hackathon beginning, we reunite and we plan on winning, no matter what obstacle we face. New members are welcome to join😀
summary:
Ares Atlas is a program which tackles the challenge of navigating Mars.

We divided the challenge into two parts:
We designed a view for mission control where there's more technology and details of the terrain meaning they can give the astronaut on the EVA more information about their surroundings. Since they have more technology, they'll also be able to detect dangers quicker which would allow them to communicate them with the astronaut quicker and help them make more calculated decisions.

However, on Mars, Wi-Fi latency usually isn't the best and therefore, we've created a HUD alongside HUD panels to further assist the astronaut.  We also implemented an AI assistant called Golden Ares AI helping the astronaut make more informed choices and acting more independently requiring mission control less often which would lead to quicker and more efficient missions.
details:
Project Overview

Imagine being an astronaut on the surface of Mars. You're several kilometres away from your habitat, surrounded by unfamiliar terrain, wearing a spacesuit that has to keep you alive in an environment that humans cannot naturally survive in. You need to know where you are, how to get back, whether your suit is functioning properly, and whether your physical condition is stable. At the same time, you may need to communicate with your team and make decisions without being able to contact Earth immediately.

This is the problem we wanted to explore with ARES ATLES.

ARES ATLES is a software-based prototype for an integrated Martian navigation and astronaut survival system. It brings together an interactive map of Mars, route-planning capabilities, physiological monitoring, spacesuit environmental monitoring, and an AI-powered mission assistant called Golden Ares AI.

The main idea behind the project is fairly straightforward: instead of making astronauts switch between several independent systems to understand what's happening around them and how they're doing, we want to bring the most important information together in one place.

One of the biggest parts of this idea is the AI assistant. We envision it as a JARVIS-inspired companion for astronauts, capable of interacting with the different components of the platform and making information easier to access. An astronaut should be able to ask about their location, request a route back to the habitat, check their health readings, or obtain a summary of their spacesuit conditions without having to manually search through multiple interfaces.

Our project explores how mapping, monitoring, data processing, and AI could work together to address some of these challenges. The current version is a prototype, and certain features represent proposed extensions rather than fully operational systems. We want to demonstrate the underlying concept while also exploring what would be required to develop it further.

Interactive Martian Map

The first major component of ARES ATLES is its interactive map of the Martian surface.

We wanted to move beyond simply displaying an image of Mars. The idea was to create a map that users can actually interact with and use to explore different regions of the planet. The mapping component incorporates relevant NASA data to provide geographical information about the Martian surface.

This is particularly important when considering the difficulties of navigation on Mars. On Earth, we are so accustomed to GPS that it is easy to take satellite-based positioning for granted. Mars, however, does not have an equivalent GPS network that astronauts can simply connect to.

A future navigation system would therefore need to establish an astronaut's position through alternative methods. These could include inertial navigation, which estimates movement using onboard motion sensors; visual navigation, which compares images of the surrounding landscape with previously recorded terrain information; and reference data obtained from orbiting spacecraft.

These approaches each have limitations. Inertial systems can accumulate errors over time, while visual navigation depends on having sufficiently recognisable terrain and suitable reference imagery. Combining multiple sources of information would therefore be important for obtaining a more reliable position estimate.

This is one of the problems we considered when developing the mapping component. A map can show where an astronaut wants to go, but a genuinely useful navigation system also needs a way to determine where that astronaut actually is.

The map also provides the geographical foundation for the route-planning component. It gives the system a way to represent destinations and the surrounding terrain, which can then be used when evaluating possible paths.

Route Planning and Navigation

Knowing the location of a destination is only part of the problem. Getting there safely is another matter entirely.

A route that looks perfectly reasonable on a map may not necessarily be suitable for an astronaut travelling across the Martian surface. The terrain could be difficult to traverse, obstacles may be present, and certain areas could introduce additional operational risks.

For this reason, we wanted to consider route planning as something more than finding the shortest distance between two points.

The system could evaluate possible routes by considering several factors, including distance, terrain difficulty, known hazards, and the resources required to complete the journey. Each section of a potential route could be assigned a cost based on these factors. The system could then compare different paths and identify the one that offers the most suitable overall result.

For example, imagine two possible routes to a habitat. The first is shorter but passes through difficult terrain, while the second is slightly longer but involves a more manageable journey. Simply choosing the shortest route would ignore an important part of the problem. A navigation system intended for astronaut use should be able to account for these differences.

Algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm and A* provide established ways of finding paths through a network of possible routes. They work by evaluating the available paths and identifying an efficient way to reach a destination. What makes this interesting for our project is the possibility of adapting the route evaluation so that it considers more than geographical distance.

We also want this component to communicate with the AI assistant. An astronaut could ask for the safest available route back to the habitat, for example, and the assistant could retrieve the relevant navigation information and explain the available route.

A more advanced version could also reconsider the route when new information becomes available. If a hazard is detected or the astronaut's available resources change, the system could evaluate whether the original route is still appropriate.

The important thing here is that navigation should be connected to the conditions under which the astronaut is travelling. A route that is suitable at the beginning of an expedition may not remain the best option throughout the journey.

The AI Mission Assistant

This is probably the component we are most excited about.

We wanted ARES ATLES to have an intelligent assistant that astronauts could actually interact with, rather than making them navigate through a complicated collection of menus every time they need information.

Our inspiration is the idea of a JARVIS-like assistant, but adapted to the practical requirements of a Mars mission. It would act as the main point of interaction between the astronaut and the different systems within ARES ATLES.

Think about the amount of information an astronaut might have to deal with during an expedition. They need to keep track of their location, monitor their physiological condition, check their spacesuit environment, communicate with their habitat, and potentially collect and interpret scientific observations. Having to access each of these functions separately could become inconvenient, particularly when the astronaut is already occupied with a task.

Golden Ares would make this interaction much simpler and quicker.

Instead of manually opening different sections of the platform, an astronaut could communicate with the assistant and request the information they need. The assistant would then use the information available from the connected components to provide an appropriate response.

For example, an astronaut could ask:

  • "Where am I currently located?"
  • "How far am I from the habitat?"
  • "Find me the safest route back."
  • "Give me a summary of my current health readings."
  • "Has my heart rate changed significantly?"
  • "What's the current oxygen availability inside my suit?"
  • "Are there any environmental readings I should be concerned about?"
  • "Summarise the observations I've collected so far."

These are examples of the kinds of interactions we want to support. The goal is to make the assistant useful for actual mission-related tasks rather than having it function as a chatbot that simply answers general questions about Mars.

Connecting the Assistant to the Map

One of the first things the assistant should be able to do is interact with the navigation system.

If an astronaut asks where they are, the assistant could retrieve the position information available to the platform. If they ask for directions, it could access the route-planning component and provide the relevant information.

More importantly, it should be able to explain the reasoning behind a suggested route. For example, it could identify that one route is shorter but involves more difficult terrain, while another offers a more suitable path based on the available geographical information.

This would make the assistant more than a voice-controlled map. It would become a way of accessing and understanding the information used by the navigation system.

Connecting the Assistant to Health Monitoring

The same idea applies to physiological monitoring.

An astronaut should be able to ask the assistant for a summary of their current readings instead of having to interpret every measurement individually.

For example, the assistant could retrieve the astronaut's heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and body temperature. It could then organise these readings into a summary and highlight any unusual changes identified by the monitoring system.

An important part of this is considering measurements together. A change in heart rate on its own does not necessarily tell the whole story. However, when considered alongside respiratory rate, blood oxygen saturation, and previous measurements, it may provide more useful information.

The assistant could explain what has changed and compare the latest readings with the astronaut's established baseline.

It would not independently diagnose medical conditions. Its role would be to make the available information easier to understand and help bring potentially important changes to the astronaut's attention.

Connecting the Assistant to Spacesuit Monitoring

The assistant would also be able to retrieve information about the environment inside the spacesuit.

This includes oxygen availability, carbon dioxide concentration, internal pressure, and temperature. These are important because the spacesuit is effectively a self-contained life-support environment.

An astronaut could ask for a summary of the suit's environmental readings and receive an explanation of the current measurements. If a reading falls outside its expected operating range, the system could highlight it.

We also want the assistant to be able to consider suit conditions alongside physiological measurements. For example, a change in oxygen availability and a simultaneous change in the astronaut's physiological readings could be more significant when considered together.

This connection between different components is one of the main things we want to achieve with ARES ATLES.

Making Information Easier to Understand

Another important part of the assistant is summarisation.

A system could collect enormous amounts of information, but presenting all of it to an astronaut at once would not necessarily be helpful. We want the assistant to make that information more accessible by identifying relevant details and communicating them in ordinary language.

Instead of simply displaying a series of measurements, it could explain which values have changed, how they compare with previous readings, and which ones may require attention.

The same principle could apply to navigation information, environmental readings, and mission updates.

In the future, we would also like to explore its use in scientific exploration. For example, an assistant connected to suitable image-processing and scientific-data tools could help astronauts examine geological features, organise observations, or compare collected images with existing information about the Martian surface.

Why an AI Assistant Is Particularly Relevant on Mars

There is another reason we consider this feature important: communication with Earth is not instantaneous.

Depending on the positions of Earth and Mars in their orbits, signals can take several minutes to travel between the planets in one direction. This means that astronauts cannot always depend on receiving immediate instructions from mission control.

A future system would therefore need to provide access to important information locally, with essential functions continuing to operate even when communication with Earth is interrupted.

We see the AI assistant as a potential part of that approach. It could work with information already available within the local system and help astronauts access it without requiring a real-time response from Earth.

Of course, this would require careful development, testing, and safeguards. The assistant would need to distinguish between reliable sensor data, missing information, and uncertain results. It should never invent a reading or present an estimate as though it were a confirmed measurement.

Ultimately, we want the assistant to feel like a useful mission companion: something that helps astronauts interact with their equipment and information, rather than another complicated system they have to manage.

Astronaut Physiological Monitoring

Another major part of ARES ATLES is its physiological monitoring component.

Exploring Mars would place astronauts in an environment that is physically demanding and very different from Earth. Their condition would need to be monitored throughout an expedition, particularly during periods of physical exertion or when they are operating far from their habitat.

We therefore wanted to include a system that can process and interpret several important physiological measurements.

The measurements we are considering include:

  • Heart rate
  • Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2)
  • Blood pressure
  • Respiratory rate
  • Body temperature

Each of these measurements provides a different piece of information.

Heart rate tells us how frequently the heart beats and can be useful when assessing physical exertion and cardiovascular activity.

Blood oxygen saturation indicates the proportion of haemoglobin in the blood that is carrying oxygen. It is useful for monitoring oxygenation, although it must be interpreted in the context of the measurement method and the astronaut's overall condition.

Blood pressure provides information about the pressure of circulating blood against arterial walls. The system can consider both systolic pressure, which is measured when the heart contracts, and diastolic pressure, which is measured when the heart relaxes.

Respiratory rate measures how frequently an astronaut breathes. Changes in breathing rate can be associated with physical activity and other physiological factors.

Body temperature is also important because the human body needs to maintain a relatively stable internal temperature to function normally.

Processing and Interpreting the Measurements

We did not want the monitoring component to be limited to displaying numbers. The idea is to process the readings so that they provide more useful information.

For heart rate, the time between successive heartbeats can be measured and used to calculate the number of beats per minute. Respiratory rate can be calculated in a similar way by counting breaths over a known time interval and converting the result into a per-minute measurement.

Blood pressure can also be used to derive additional indicators. For example, the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure gives pulse pressure. An estimate of mean arterial pressure can be calculated by combining the two readings, with greater weight given to diastolic pressure because the heart spends more time in its relaxed phase than in its contraction phase.

The system can also examine how readings change over time.

This is important because physiological measurements naturally vary between individuals. Two astronauts may have different normal resting heart rates, for example. Comparing every astronaut against the same fixed value would therefore not always provide a useful assessment.

Instead, the system could establish a baseline using an astronaut's previous readings and compare new measurements against that baseline. It could also examine how quickly a value is changing, since a sudden change may be more noteworthy than a small variation over a longer period.

By considering the measurements in this way, the monitoring component can provide more context than a simple display of individual readings.

Alerts and the AI Assistant

The physiological monitoring component is intended to work directly with the AI assistant.

If a reading falls outside a defined operating range or differs significantly from an astronaut's usual measurements, the system could highlight the change.

The assistant could then explain which measurement has changed, how it compares with previous readings, and whether other measurements have changed at the same time.

This is particularly useful because astronauts may not always have the time to examine every measurement individually while carrying out an activity.

The system is intended for monitoring and decision support, not medical diagnosis. Any actual medical response would still require appropriate procedures and qualified personnel.

Spacesuit Environmental Monitoring

Monitoring the astronaut is only one part of the problem. We also need to consider the environment in which the astronaut is operating.

A spacesuit is not simply protective clothing. It is a life-support system that maintains conditions necessary for a human being to survive outside a pressurised habitat.

For this reason, ARES ATLES also considers the monitoring of environmental conditions inside the suit.

Some of the important measurements include:

  • Oxygen availability
  • Carbon dioxide concentration
  • Internal pressure
  • Temperature

Oxygen availability is essential because the astronaut depends on the suit's life-support system to provide a breathable environment.

Carbon dioxide is equally important to monitor because it is produced when the astronaut breathes and must be removed from the breathing environment. If its concentration becomes excessive, it can create serious risks.

Pressure is another critical factor. The atmospheric pressure on Mars is far too low for an unprotected human to survive, so the spacesuit must maintain an appropriate internal pressure.

Temperature monitoring is also necessary because the Martian environment can expose astronauts to significant thermal challenges.

Why Suit Monitoring and Health Monitoring Need to Work Together

One thing we particularly wanted to consider was the relationship between the astronaut's physiological condition and the conditions inside the suit.

These two categories of information are closely connected, but they are not interchangeable.

For example, oxygen availability inside the suit describes the environment supplying the astronaut with breathable gas. Blood oxygen saturation, on the other hand, describes how much oxygen is being carried by haemoglobin in the bloodstream. They measure different things and should not be confused.

Having access to both types of information could help provide a more complete picture of the astronaut's condition.

The AI assistant could retrieve the readings from both components and present them together when an astronaut requests a status report.

This is one of the ways in which we want the different parts of ARES ATLES to complement each other.

Communication with the Martian Habitat

During an expedition, astronauts would need to maintain communication with their habitat and other mission-support systems.

ARES ATLES considers how information from the astronaut's navigation and monitoring systems could be made available to a nearby habitat.

This could include the astronaut's location, physiological readings, suit environmental measurements, and mission observations.

In a future implementation, these measurements could be transmitted as telemetry, allowing habitat personnel to monitor the astronaut's status and maintain awareness of ongoing surface activities.

We also considered the problem of communication with Earth. The considerable distance between the two planets means that communication delays are unavoidable. In certain situations, waiting for instructions from Earth may not be practical.

This is why we consider local communication and processing important. A future version of the platform should ideally be able to access essential information and carry out important monitoring functions without relying entirely on a continuous connection to Earth.

The assistant could also use information available locally, allowing astronauts to interact with the system even when communication with Earth is temporarily unavailable.

Emergency Situations and Combined Decision-Making

One of the reasons we wanted to integrate all these features is that emergencies rarely involve just one problem.

Imagine an astronaut travelling away from the habitat. They encounter difficult terrain, their physical condition begins to change, and they need to return. A navigation system alone might be able to calculate a route, while a health-monitoring system might be able to identify unusual physiological readings. However, neither system necessarily provides the full context needed to make a decision.

This is where connecting the components becomes useful.

ARES ATLES explores how information from the map, route planner, physiological monitor, and spacesuit monitor could be brought together.

The astronaut could request a summary of their condition and available route options through the AI assistant. The system could then present the relevant information, allowing the astronaut to make a more informed decision.

In a more advanced version, route planning could account for the astronaut's available resources and physical condition. For example, a route requiring less physical exertion might be preferable when the astronaut is already fatigued, provided that the geographical information supports that choice.

Similarly, if an environmental warning is received, the navigation component could be used to identify alternative paths where suitable data is available.

We do not claim that the current prototype can autonomously manage every emergency scenario. Rather, we are exploring how a connected system could provide useful information when several different factors need to be considered at once.

Helmet-Mounted Heads-Up Display

We also considered how astronauts would actually interact with ARES ATLES while wearing a spacesuit.

A conventional computer interface would not necessarily be practical during an expedition. Astronauts may be handling equipment, collecting samples, or navigating difficult terrain. Constantly looking away to operate a separate device could be inconvenient.

This led us to consider a helmet-mounted heads-up display.

The idea is to project important information onto the astronaut's visor, allowing them to view relevant data while remaining aware of their surroundings.

A future interface could display navigation directions, the astronaut's location, distance to the habitat, physiological readings, suit environmental conditions, and important notifications.

The AI assistant would complement this by allowing astronauts to request information conversationally rather than manually navigating through different screens.

For example, an astronaut could request a health summary or ask for directions while continuing to view the terrain around them.

The HUD is currently a proposed interface concept rather than a fully developed physical spacesuit display. Our focus is on exploring what information should be available and how the different components could contribute to such an interface.

What Makes ARES ATLES Different?

We are aware that many of the individual technologies involved in this project already exist. Planetary mapping, pathfinding algorithms, physiological monitoring, environmental sensors, and AI assistants are all established areas of technology.

What interested us was the possibility of bringing them together in a way that is specifically relevant to human exploration on Mars.

For example, a navigation system might normally focus on geographical information. A health-monitoring system might focus on physiological readings. A spacesuit monitoring system might deal with oxygen, pressure, and temperature.

However, an astronaut does not experience these things separately. They are all part of the same mission, and changes in one area can affect decisions in another.

We wanted to explore a system in which these components can communicate with one another, with the AI assistant acting as the main way for astronauts to access and understand the information.

The JARVIS-inspired assistant is particularly important here. Rather than being an additional feature placed alongside the map and monitoring tools, it is intended to connect them through a single interaction system.

We also wanted to consider the realities of operating on Mars, especially the absence of conventional GPS, the communication delay with Earth, and the need for astronauts to access useful information while working in an unfamiliar environment.

The project is therefore less about inventing an entirely new individual technology and more about exploring how existing approaches could be combined into a useful system for a future Mars mission.

Tools and Development

ARES ATLES is being developed as a software-based prototype.

Our work involves developing the interactive Martian mapping interface, incorporating relevant NASA data, implementing the monitoring and calculation components, and exploring how the AI assistant can interact with the different parts of the platform.

The mapping component uses NASA-sourced geographical information to provide a basis for exploring the Martian surface.

The navigation component draws on established pathfinding approaches, including algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm and A*, to explore how routes can be evaluated and compared.

The physiological monitoring component involves processing numerical readings, calculating derived indicators, comparing measurements over time, and identifying changes that may require attention.

The spacesuit monitoring component focuses on the environmental measurements that would be relevant to maintaining a suitable life-support environment.

The AI assistant is being developed as the interaction layer connecting these different functions. Its intended role is to retrieve available information, respond to mission-related requests, and present information in a form that is easier to understand.

The helmet-mounted display is a proposed extension of the interface rather than a claim that we have developed physical spacesuit hardware.

Challenges and Factors We Considered

There were several things we needed to consider while developing the concept.

The first was navigation. We cannot simply assume that an astronaut on Mars would have access to the same positioning infrastructure that we use on Earth. Any realistic navigation system would need to account for alternative positioning methods and the possibility of accumulated errors.

Another challenge is the reliability of the information being used. A system that provides health or environmental information is only useful if its inputs are sufficiently reliable. Missing measurements, inaccurate sensors, or communication interruptions could all affect the quality of the information presented.

We also considered how different measurements should be interpreted. A single physiological reading may not provide enough information to understand an astronaut's condition, which is why comparisons with previous measurements and the consideration of multiple readings are important.

Communication delays were another major consideration. A future Mars-support system should not depend entirely on receiving immediate instructions from Earth.

Finally, we had to distinguish between what can realistically be demonstrated in a software prototype and what would require additional hardware or infrastructure. Actual spacesuit sensor integration, a physical helmet-mounted display, and operational Martian positioning infrastructure would require further development and testing.

We want to be clear about these limitations because they are part of the engineering problem itself. Developing a concept is one thing; making it reliable enough for an environment such as Mars is another.

Conclusion

ARES ATLES started with a question: what would an astronaut actually need while exploring the surface of Mars, and how could we make those different systems work together?

Our answer is a platform that combines navigation, geographical information, health monitoring, spacesuit environmental monitoring, and an AI-powered assistant.

The interactive map provides the geographical foundation. The route-planning component explores how astronauts could navigate more intelligently. The monitoring systems provide information about both the astronaut and their immediate environment. The AI assistant brings these functions together and gives astronauts a more accessible way to interact with the platform.

We are particularly interested in developing the assistant beyond a conventional chatbot. We want it to understand the context of the mission by accessing information from the systems connected to it and helping astronauts make sense of that information.

ARES ATLES is currently a prototype, and there is considerable room for further development. However, we believe that exploring the integration of these technologies is a worthwhile step towards understanding how future astronauts could be supported during human exploration of Mars.
